title: Rate limiter as Express middleware
idea: In a Node.js service the rate limiter becomes middleware: it keys each request, asks the limiter, and either calls `next()` or answers 429 with a retry hint.
points: Middleware picks the key, such as an API key header, before any handler runs.
Rejected calls get 429 and a `Retry-After` header, in seconds.
Follow-up: in-memory limits are per process; N instances allow N times the limit.
A shared counter in PostgreSQL enforces one limit across instances with one atomic upsert.

steps.caption: A client sends a search request with its API key.
The middleware runs first and reads the key from the `X-Api-Key` header.
It asks the limiter for a decision. The bucket for key-A still has tokens.
Allowed: the middleware sets `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and calls `next()`.
Later key-A has spent every token. The limiter answers no.
The middleware stops the chain and replies 429 with `Retry-After`. The handler never runs.

code.title: Express middleware
code.caption: A token bucket per API key in one Express process, with an injected clock. Tokens are integer milli-tokens, as on the Java page. The demo trusts the X-Api-Key header to stay short. In production, run authentication middleware first and key on the verified identity it sets.

walk.text: The limiter takes capacity, refill rate and a clock function.
Lazy refill: ms elapsed times tokens per second is milli-tokens, capped at capacity.
Spend a token, or report how long until one returns.
The middleware sets headers, then calls `next()` or replies 429.
Capacity 3 per key; only routes under /api are limited.
Four calls from key-A, one from key-B, then key-A one second later.

code.title: One limit across instances
code.caption: A fixed window counter in PostgreSQL, chosen because it fits one atomic upsert. Ten parallel requests race, and the database lets exactly the limit through.

walk.text: One row per key and window; the CHECK keeps hits positive.
Insert the first hit, or add one only while hits stay below the limit.
No returned row means the window is full: reject.
Ten requests in parallel over pooled connections, as if from several instances.
A new window starts a fresh row, so the key is allowed again.

pitfalls: Key only on verified identities; a raw client header lets callers rotate keys and skip limits.
Follow-up: decide fail-open or fail-closed when the shared store is down.
Behind a proxy, `req.ip` is the proxy unless you configure `trust proxy`.

options: It changes from run to run
quiz.why: Conflicting upserts on one row run one after another. The update's WHERE sees the true count, so only five succeed.

takeaway: Limit in middleware; share the counter when the service runs on many instances.
